title: Caribbean Chicken Curry
subtitle: Trinidad-style coconut milk chicken curry with potato
excerpt: Caribbean chicken curry arrived in the islands with Indian indentured labourers in the 19th century and developed its own distinct identity. Coconut milk, allspice, and whole scotch bonnet chilli give it a flavour quite different from Indian versions. The potato absorbs the sauce and makes it filling.
sourceNotes: Curry arrived in the Caribbean with Indian indentured labourers who were brought to Trinidad and other islands from 1845 onwards after the abolition of slavery. Caribbean curry developed separately from Indian curry over generations, adopting local ingredients like scotch bonnet, allspice, and coconut milk.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze without the coconut milk. Reheat and stir in fresh coconut milk to finish.

content.text: A whole scotch bonnet chilli added to the pot without cutting gives mild heat and flavour without turning the curry very spicy. Pricking it with a knife before adding gives more heat. Remove it before serving if you want a gentler result.

items.prepNote: use a 400ml tin of coconut milk
or 1 whole scotch bonnet chilli, uncut

content.text: Heat the oil in a large pot over high heat. Brown the chicken on all sides for 5 minutes. Remove and set aside.
Cook the onion in the same pot for 7 minutes until golden. Add the garlic and ginger. Cook 2 minutes.
Add the cumin, turmeric, and allspice. Stir for 1 minute. Add the chilli.
Return the chicken. Add the stock and coconut milk. Season with salt.
Bring to a simmer. Add the potato. Cover and cook on low heat for 30 minutes.
Remove the lid and cook for 10 more minutes until the sauce thickens and the potato is soft. Taste and adjust salt. Serve with rice.

items.cause: Coconut milk is rich and sweet; spices may be under-seasoned
items.fix: Add a squeeze of lemon juice and a little more cumin to balance

items.symptom: Potato is still hard after 30 minutes
items.cause: Cut too large or heat too low
items.fix: Cut potato into smaller 2cm cubes and check the simmer is active, not just warm
Once coconut milk is in, keep the heat to a gentle simmer and avoid boiling vigorously

content.text: Caribbean chicken curry is found across the islands. In Trinidad, it is closely tied to Indo-Trinidadian cooking. Indian indentured workers brought their curry traditions to the Caribbean in the 19th century. Today it is eaten at roti shops and family tables across the region.
